claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on EleNRMT.

claims.claim: NRATs form a small clade in plants whose evolutionary relationship to classical SLC11 transporters is much closer than prokaryotic NRMTs.
claims.source: Besides the prokaryotic NRMTs, which constitute a large branch of the family that is distantly related to transition metal ion transporters of the same family, the NRATs form a small clade in plants, whose evolutionary relationship to classical SLC11 transporters is much closer (Ramanadane et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: NRATs have evolved to combat Al3+ toxicity in soil.
claims.source: These proteins have evolved to combat Al3+ toxicity in soil (Chauhan et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on NRATs.

claims.claim: Al3+ as a strong Lewis acid strongly interacts with membranes to compromise their integrity.
claims.source: As strong Lewis acid, this trivalent cation strongly interacts with membranes to compromise their integrity.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the chemical properties of Al3+.

claims.claim: NRATs were proposed to catalyze Al3+ uptake into the cytoplasm of root cells acting in concert with other proteins, which mediate the further transport into vacuoles where it is neutralized by the complexation with dicarboxylates.
claims.source: As one of the mechanisms to neutralize the adverse effect of Al3+, NRATs were proposed to catalyze its uptake into the cytoplasm of root cells acting in concert with other proteins, which mediate the further transport into vacuoles where it is neutralized by the complexation with dicarboxylates (Xia et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on NRATs.

claims.claim: SiNRAT broadly transports divalent transition metal ions by a mechanism that is not coupled to protons.
claims.source: We show that this protein broadly transports divalent transition metal ions by a mechanism that is not coupled to protons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in the manuscript.

claims.claim: SiNRAT shares the hallmarks of the SLC11 family.
claims.source: The cryo-EM structure of SiNRAT displays a protein that shares the hallmarks of the SLC11 family.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claims.claim: The SiNRAT structure harbors an ion binding region for Al3+ located inside an aqueous pocket.
claims.source: This structure harbors an ion binding region for Al3+ located inside an aqueous pocket, which encompasses the predicted replacements of coordinating residues and which also contains an additional acidic amino acid that increases the negative charge density of the site to accommodate the larger net charge of the transported substrate.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claims.claim: The ion binding region of SiNRAT contains an additional acidic amino acid that increases the negative charge density of the site to accommodate the larger net charge of the transported substrate.
claims.source: This structure harbors an ion binding region for Al3+ located inside an aqueous pocket, which encompasses the predicted replacements of coordinating residues and which also contains an additional acidic amino acid that increases the negative charge density of the site to accommodate the larger net charge of the transported substrate.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and inference about the role of the acidic residue.

claims.claim: Seven homologues of the prototypic NRAT1 from Oryza sativa were identified in Blast searches of eukaryotic sequence databases.
claims.source: In the course of a previous phylogenetic analysis, we were able to spot seven homologues of the prototypic NRAT1 from Oryza sativa (XP_015625418.1, Uniprot: Q6ZG85) in Blast searches of eukaryotic sequence databases (Ramanadane et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: All identified NRAT proteins contain the described hallmarks of NRATs, which distinguishes this clade of the SLC11 family from the bulk of transition metal ion transporters.
claims.source: All identified proteins contain the described hallmarks of NRATs, which distinguishes this clade of the SLC11 family from the bulk of transition metal ion transporters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Differences in NRATs include variations in the putative ion coordinating site, where the conserved DPGN motif on α1 of classical NRAMPs is changed to DPSN.
claims.source: Differences include variations in the putative ion coordinating site, where the conserved DPGN motif on α1 of classical NRAMPs is changed to DPSN and the A/CxxM motif on α6 to AxxT (Lu et al., 2018; Ramanadane et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on NRATs.

claims.claim: The A/CxxM motif on α6 of classical NRAMPs is changed to AxxT in NRATs.
claims.source: Differences include variations in the putative ion coordinating site, where the conserved DPGN motif on α1 of classical NRAMPs is changed to DPSN and the A/CxxM motif on α6 to AxxT (Lu et al., 2018; Ramanadane et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on NRATs.

claims.claim: The conserved methionine in classical NRAMPs is replaced with a threonine in NRATs, which offers a hard oxygen ligand for metal ion interactions.
claims.source: Latter replaces the conserved methionine, whose sulfur atom is involved in transition metal ion coordination, with a threonine, which offers a hard oxygen ligand for metal ion interactions.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on inference from sequence analysis and knowledge of coordination chemistry.

claims.claim: SiNRAT from S. italica was selected as the biochemically best behaving homologue based on the monodispersity of the eluted peak in fluorescence size exclusion chromatography.
claims.source: These experiments have singled out the protein from S. italica (termed SiNRAT, XP_004952002.1) as construct with comparably high expression level and promising biochemical behavior.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence size exclusion chromatography.

claims.claim: SiNRAT was purified in the detergent n-dodecyl-β-D-maltopyranoside (DDM).
claims.source: We have subsequently scaled up the expression of SiNRAT in suspension culture and purified it in the detergent n-dodecyl-β-D-maltopyranoside (DDM) for further studies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B.

claims.claim: SiNRAT-mediated Mn2+ transport saturates with an apparent Km of about 14 µM.
claims.source: Transport is strongly dependent on the Mn2+ concentration and saturates with an apparent Km of about 14 µM, reflecting the binding of the transported substrate to a saturable site (Figure 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in Figure 1A and B.

claims.claim: Ca2+ and Mg2+ show concentration-dependent competition with Mn2+ transport by SiNRAT, which is indicative for their specific binding to the protein.
claims.source: We subsequently investigated impairment of Mn2+ transport by the alkaline earth metal ions Ca2+ and Mg2+ and found a concentration-dependent competition by both ions, which is indicative for their specific binding to the protein (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from competition assays shown in the figures.

claims.claim: SiNRAT mediates the uptake of Ca2+ and Mg2+ into proteoliposomes.
claims.source: To investigate whether they would also be transported, we directly monitored their influx into proteoliposomes employing the fluorophores Fura-2 for the detection of Ca2+ and Magnesium Green for Mg2+. In both cases, we found a weak signal that saturates at µM concentrations, which reflects uptake of both ions (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in the figures.

claims.claim: SiNRAT acts as uncoupled transporter that facilitates the bidirectional transport of metal ions with poor selectivity.
claims.source: These findings suggest that, akin to the Mg2+ transporter EleNRMT, SiNRAT acts as uncoupled transporter that facilitates the bidirectional transport of metal ions with poor selectivity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing lack of proton coupling.

claims.claim: All transport experiments with SiNRAT were carried out at neutral pH.
claims.source: Although, in a physiological context, SiNRAT presumably operates at mildly acidic extracellular conditions (i.e. at a pH <5.5), all transport experiments were carried out at neutral pH since this resulted in maximum proteoliposome stability and highest sensitivity of the employed fluorophores.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions used in the study.

claims.claim: Ga3+ inhibits Mn2+ transport by SiNRAT, which emphasizes its interaction with the transporter.
claims.source: In an assay to investigate the interference with Mn2+ transport, we found an inhibition by Ga3+, which emphasizes its interaction with the transporter (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from competition assays shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Ga3+ does not act as non-specific inhibitor of the SLC11 family, as it did not show competition with the prokaryotic transition metal ion transporter EcoDMT.
claims.source: Conversely, we did not observe such competition with the prokaryotic transition metal ion transporter EcoDMT, excluding the action of Ga3+ as non-specific inhibitor of the family (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from competition assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I.

claims.claim: ITC experiments showed a specific signal upon Al3+ titration as a consequence of its interaction with SiNRAT.
claims.source: Since equivalent studies with Al3+ are prevented by its disruptive properties on membrane integrity, we used isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) to investigate the binding of the ion to SiNRAT in detergent solution. These experiments showed a specific signal upon Al3+ titration as a consequence of its interaction with the transporter (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ITC experiments shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: At neutral pH, trivalent Al3+ is at equilibrium with its hydroxyl complexes, which complicates data analysis.
claims.source: However, at the neutral pH of the sample, the trivalent ion is at equilibrium with its hydroxyl complexes, which complicates data analysis (Kiss, 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about Al3+ chemistry, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The ITC thermograms for Al3+ binding to SiNRAT were best fitted to a sum of two binding constants, both in the low micromolar range.
claims.source: The thermograms were thus best fitted to a sum of two binding constants, both in the low micromolar range (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ITC experiments shown in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: No evidence for metal ion concentration-dependent decrease of ACMA fluorescence was detected for SiNRAT with Mn2+, Ca2+, Mg2+ or Ga3+, suggesting that SiNRAT acts as uncoupled transporter.
claims.source: To this end, we have assayed the import of H+ at increasing concentrations of the transported ions Mn2+, Ca2+, Mg2+ and the putative substrate Ga3+ but did in no case detect evidence for metal ion concentration-dependent decrease of ACMA fluorescence, despite the negative membrane potential established by an outwardly directed K+ gradient, which would facilitate H+ transport (Figure 1K and L, Figure 1—figure supplement 2J, K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from proton transport assays shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The nanobody Nb1SiNRAT inhibits Mn2+ transport in a concentration-dependent manner when added to the outside of liposomes.
claims.source: The procedure allowed the identification of the nanobody Nb1SiNRAT (short Nb1) as promising interaction partner that does not dissociate during size exclusion chromatography, and which inhibits Mn2+ transport in a concentration-dependent manner when added to the outside of liposomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The incomplete inhibition of transport by Nb1 presumably reflects the mixed distribution of reconstituted SiNRAT residing in either inside-out or outside-out orientation.
claims.source: The incomplete inhibition of transport by Nb1 presumably reflects the mixed distribution of reconstituted SiNRAT residing in either inside-out or outside-out orientation, where the epitopes recognized by the nanobody are only accessible in one orientation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation of incomplete inhibition.

claims.claim: A cryo-EM density map of the SiNRAT-Nb1 complex was obtained at 3.66 Å resolution.
claims.source: For the SiNRAT-Nb1 complex, we have prepared samples for cryo-EM. Since data recorded in the detergent DDM did not permit a 3D reconstruction at high resolution, we have reconstituted the complex into amphipols (Kleinschmidt and Popot, 2014) and collected a large dataset, which ultimately yielded a cryo-EM density map at 3.66 Å (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3, Table 1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cryo-EM analysis.

claims.claim: The sample used for cryo-EM imaging did not contain transported ions due to challenges associated with the amphipol reconstitution process.
claims.source: Due to the challenges associated with the amphipol reconstitution process, the sample used for imaging did not contain transported ions. In case of trivalent ions this would have required a lowering of the pH to increase their solubility, which was incompatible with nanobody binding.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions used in the study.

claims.claim: The cryo-EM map of SiNRAT was of high quality and allowed the unambiguous interpretation with an atomic model revealing details of the 3D organization of SiNRAT.
claims.source: The resulting map was of high quality and allowed the unambiguous interpretation with an atomic model revealing details of the 3D organization of SiNRAT (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the quality of the cryo-EM map and the resulting model.

claims.claim: The SiNRAT structure shows a protein sharing the conserved architecture of the SLC11 family with a core consisting of a pair of structurally related repeats of five transmembrane spanning segments.
claims.source: The SiNRAT structure in complex with Nb1 is depicted in Figure 2. It shows a protein sharing the conserved architecture of the SLC11 family with a core consisting of a pair of structurally related repeats of five transmembrane spanning segments that are oriented in the membrane with opposite directions in an arrangement that was initially observed in the amino acid transporter LeuT (Yamashita et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis and comparison with other structures.

claims.claim: The unwound centers of the first helix of each repeat together constitute a substrate binding site in SiNRAT.
claims.source: In this architecture, the unwound centers of the first helix of each repeat together constitute a substrate binding site (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claims.claim: SiNRAT contains a total of 12 membrane-inserted helices akin to other eukaryotic family members and the prokaryotic EcoDMT.
claims.source: The protein contains a total of 12 membrane-inserted helices akin to other eukaryotic family members and the prokaryotic EcoDMT (PDBID: 5M87) (Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017), whose Cα-positions superimpose with an RMSD of 2.66 Å (Figures 2B and 3A, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis and comparison with other structures.

claims.claim: The Cα-positions of SiNRAT and EcoDMT superimpose with an RMSD of 2.66 Å.
claims.source: The protein contains a total of 12 membrane-inserted helices akin to other eukaryotic family members and the prokaryotic EcoDMT (PDBID: 5M87) (Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017), whose Cα-positions superimpose with an RMSD of 2.66 Å (Figures 2B and 3A, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claims.claim: The nanobody Nb1 binds to an extended interface located at the extracellular side of SiNRAT.
claims.source: The nanobody binds to an extended interface located at the extracellular side. These interactions involve contacts of all three CDRs of the nanobody, which bridge the core domain of SiNRAT consisting of α-helices 1–10 with α-helices 11–12 located at its periphery, thereby contacting the loops α1–2, α5–6, α7–8 and residues on α11 and burying 1682 Å2 of the combined molecular surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claims.claim: The nanobody Nb1 interactions with SiNRAT bury 1682 Å2 of the combined molecular surface.
claims.source: The nanobody binds to an extended interface located at the extracellular side. These interactions involve contacts of all three CDRs of the nanobody, which bridge the core domain of SiNRAT consisting of α-helices 1–10 with α-helices 11–12 located at its periphery, thereby contacting the loops α1–2, α5–6, α7–8 and residues on α11 and burying 1682 Å2 of the combined molecular surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claims.claim: In the SiNRAT-Nb1 complex, α11 and α12 are detached from the core domain on the extracellular part in a conformation that is presumably stabilized by Nb1 binding.
claims.source: Unlike in EcoDMT, in this complex α11 and α12 are detached from the core domain on the extracellular part in a conformation that is presumably stabilized by Nb1 binding (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, C).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on structural data and inference about the role of Nb1 binding.

claims.claim: The SiNRAT structure resembles an inward-occluded state of the classical SLC11 transporter DraNRAMP.
claims.source: The observed structure resembles an inward-occluded state of the classical SLC11 transporter DraNRAMP (PDBID: 8E60, DraNRAMPocc), where most of the structure retains a conformation observed in the inward-facing structure of the same protein (PDBID: 6D9W, DraNRAMPinw) except for a movement of the intracellular part of α-helix 1 (α1a), which has rearranged to close the access path to the ion binding site (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B; Bozzi et al., 2019b; Ray et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claims.claim: The RMSD of Cα atoms upon superposition of SiNRAT with DraNRAMPocc is 1.57 Å.
claims.source: This resemblance is reflected in an RMSD of Cα atoms of 1.57 Å upon a superposition of SiNRAT with DraNRAMPocc and 1.74 Å with DraNRAMPinw, whereas the RMSD of 2.71 Å compared to the outward-facing conformation of the same protein (PDBID: 6BU5, DraNRAMPout) is considerably larger (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claims.claim: The RMSD of Cα atoms upon superposition of SiNRAT with DraNRAMPinw is 1.74 Å.
claims.source: This resemblance is reflected in an RMSD of Cα atoms of 1.57 Å upon a superposition of SiNRAT with DraNRAMPocc and 1.74 Å with DraNRAMPinw, whereas the RMSD of 2.71 Å compared to the outward-facing conformation of the same protein (PDBID: 6BU5, DraNRAMPout) is considerably larger (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claims.claim: The RMSD of Cα atoms upon superposition of SiNRAT with DraNRAMPout is 2.71 Å.
claims.source: This resemblance is reflected in an RMSD of Cα atoms of 1.57 Å upon a superposition of SiNRAT with DraNRAMPocc and 1.74 Å with DraNRAMPinw, whereas the RMSD of 2.71 Å compared to the outward-facing conformation of the same protein (PDBID: 6BU5, DraNRAMPout) is considerably larger (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claims.claim: The shorter α1a of SiNRAT is located closer to α6b compared to DraNRAMPinw, resulting in a narrowing of an aqueous cavity leading toward the supposed ion binding site.
claims.source: As in DraNRAMPocc, the shorter α1a of SiNRAT is located closer to α6b compared to DraNRAMPinw, resulting in a narrowing of an aqueous cavity leading toward the supposed ion binding site, thereby separating this site from the intracellular environment (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claims.claim: The SiNRAT structure represents an intermediate between both endpoints of a transporter, functioning by an alternate access mechanism, that is closer to an inward-facing state.
claims.source: We thus assume that the SiNRAT structure represents an intermediate between both endpoints of a transporter, functioning by an alternate access mechanism, that is closer to an inward-facing state.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison data.

claims.claim: In the SiNRAT structure, the binding site is sealed to both sides of the membrane by a thin gate toward the inside and a thick gate toward the outside.
claims.source: In its conformation, the binding site is sealed to both sides of the membrane by a thin gate composed of a single layer of residues (i.e. Asp 66, Asp 140, Thr 241, Tyr 243, and Thr 346) toward the inside and a thick gate (encompassing several layers of residues and spanning about 15 Å) toward the outside (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claims.claim: Residual cryo-EM density bridging the neighboring residues Asp 66 and Ser 68 in SiNRAT presumably originates from water, Na+, or traces of divalent metal ions.
claims.source: Although for the reasons described above, we have not explicitly added transported ions to our sample, we find residual cryo-EM density bridging the neighboring residues Asp 66 and Ser 68 which, as part of the supposed ion binding site, are both located on the unwound loop connecting α1a and α1b (Figure 4A). This density presumably either originates from water, the monovalent cation Na+ that is contained in the sample at a concentration of 200 mM, or traces of divalent metal ions found in our solution.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the origin of the observed density.

claims.claim: Asp 66 is universally conserved and was shown to constitute a key component for ion coordination in the entire SLC11 family.
claims.source: In this putative site, Asp 66 is particularly striking, since it is universally conserved and was shown to constitute a key component for ion coordination in the entire SLC11 family.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the SLC11 family.

claims.claim: Ser 68 is unique to NRATs and substituted by a Gly in all other members of the SLC11 family.
claims.source: In contrast, Ser 68 is unique to NRATs and substituted by a Gly in all other members (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In both SiNRAT and DraNRAMPocc structures, the water-filled paths to the metal ion binding site are sealed from both sides of the membrane.
claims.source: In both structures, the water-filled paths to the metal ion binding site are sealed from both sides of the membrane and bound ions would thus be segregated from their aqueous environment, although the occlusion toward the intracellular solution is more pronounced in DraNRAMPocc (Figures 3C, 4B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claims.claim: In DraNRAMPocc, the interacting transition metal ion is predominantly enclosed by protein residues except for one contact with a small pocket harboring trapped water molecules.
claims.source: In its binding site, the interacting transition metal ion in DraNRAMPocc is predominantly enclosed by protein residues except for one contact with a small pocket harboring trapped water molecules (Ray et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on DraNRAMP.

claims.claim: The side chains of Asp 56 and Asn 59 on α1, in conjunction with the backbone carbonyls of Ala 53 and Ala 227, tightly surround the bound Mn2+ in DraNRAMPocc.
claims.source: The side chains of Asp 56 and Asn 59 on α1, in conjunction with the backbone carbonyls of Ala 53 and Ala 227, tightly surround the bound Mn2+. Additionally, the thioether group of Met 230 contributes a soft ligand for ion interactions (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from DraNRAMP.

claims.claim: The thioether group of Met 230 contributes a soft ligand for ion interactions in DraNRAMPocc.
claims.source: The side chains of Asp 56 and Asn 59 on α1, in conjunction with the backbone carbonyls of Ala 53 and Ala 227, tightly surround the bound Mn2+. Additionally, the thioether group of Met 230 contributes a soft ligand for ion interactions (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from DraNRAMP.

claims.claim: A water-mediated interaction with the side chain of Gln 378 on α10 completes the octahedral coordination of the ion in DraNRAMPocc.
claims.source: Finally, a water-mediated interaction with the side chain of Gln 378 on α10 completes the octahedral coordination of the ion (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from DraNRAMP.

claims.claim: The equivalent region to the DraNRAMP binding site in SiNRAT contains an elongated, approximately cylindrical pocket of predominant polar character that is about 10 Å long and 4–5 Å wide.
claims.source: In contrast, the equivalent region in SiNRAT contains an elongated, approximately cylindrical pocket of predominant polar character that is about 10 Å long and 4–5 Å wide and that encloses a three times larger volume than in DraNRAMP (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claims.claim: The pocket in the SiNRAT binding region encloses a three times larger volume than in DraNRAMP.
claims.source: In contrast, the equivalent region in SiNRAT contains an elongated, approximately cylindrical pocket of predominant polar character that is about 10 Å long and 4–5 Å wide and that encloses a three times larger volume than in DraNRAMP (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claims.claim: Residues of the consensus binding site in SiNRAT include Asp 66, Ser 68, and Asn 69 on α1, and Ala 238 and Thr 241 on α6.
claims.source: Despite the inability to pinpoint the exact location of bound ions, we find residues of the consensus binding site to line about half of this pocket (Figure 4B). These include the previously mentioned Asp 66 and Ser 68, both bordering residual density in our cryo-EM data and the conserved Asn 69, all located on α1. On α6, the interacting residues include the conserved Ala 238, whose backbone carbonyl points toward the pocket and Thr 241, which replaces the conserved methionine in NRAMP transporters and whose side chain could contribute a hard ligand for either direct or water-mediated ion interactions (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claims.claim: Thr 241 in SiNRAT replaces the conserved methionine in NRAMP transporters and could contribute a hard ligand for either direct or water-mediated ion interactions.
claims.source: On α6, the interacting residues include the conserved Ala 238, whose backbone carbonyl points toward the pocket and Thr 241, which replaces the conserved methionine in NRAMP transporters and whose side chain could contribute a hard ligand for either direct or water-mediated ion interactions (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on structural data and inference about the role of Thr 241.

claims.claim: The glutamine on α10 involved in ion binding in DraNRAMP is replaced by a serine (Ser 403) in SiNRAT, whose shorter side chain does not contact the aqueous pocket.
claims.source: Distinct from DraNRAMP, the glutamine on α10 involved in ion binding is replaced by a serine (Ser 403), whose shorter side chain does not contact the aqueous pocket and thus would not be available for metal ion interactions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claims.claim: The acidic side chain of Asp 140 located on α3 in SiNRAT lines the cavity close to the predicted ion binding site.
claims.source: Instead, we find the acidic side chain of Asp 140 located on α3 to line the cavity, close to the predicted ion binding site, at a position that contains a threonine (Thr 130) in DraNRAMP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claims.claim: Asp 140 is conserved in NRATs and would increase the negative charge density of the region by offering favorable coulombic interactions that stabilize the additional positive charge of Al3+.
claims.source: This acidic side chain, which is conserved in NRATs, would increase the negative charge density of the region by offering favorable coulombic interactions that stabilize the additional positive charge of Al3+ (Figure 4B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on structural data and inference about the role of Asp 140.

claims.claim: Besides the replacement of the conserved methionine of the transition metal ion binding site, SiNRAT has an expanded interaction region with increased polar character and negative charge density, which together may account for the altered substrate preference and stabilize trivalent cations.
claims.source: Thus, besides the replacement of the conserved methionine of the transition metal ion binding site, we find an expanded interaction region with increased polar character and negative charge density, which together may account for the altered substrate preference and stabilize trivalent cations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural data about the binding site.

claims.claim: Mutation of Asp 66 or Asn 69 to alanine severely compromised transport of Mn2+ by SiNRAT.
claims.source: Upon mutation of the residues Asp 66 or Asn 69 to alanine, we found a severely compromised transport of Mn2+, consistent with equivalent results obtained for other pro- and eukaryotic transition metal ion transporters (Figure 5B and C; Bozzi et al., 2019b; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2014; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017; Ramanadane et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: Mutation of Thr 241 to alanine or valine strongly negatively impacted Mn2+ transport by SiNRAT.
claims.source: In this case, we have mutated the residue to alanine to truncate the side chain and valine to preserve its volume but remove its polar character. In both cases, we found a similar strong negative impact of the respective mutations on Mn2+ transport (Figure 5D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in Figure 5D and E.

claims.claim: The mutant T241V of SiNRAT did not show any specific heat exchange upon Al3+ titration in ITC experiments, emphasizing the importance of the residue for Al3+ interactions.
claims.source: For this residue, we were also interested in whether a mutation would affect interactions with trivalent cations and thus investigated binding of Al3+ to the mutant T241V by ITC. Unlike WT, we did not detect any specific heat exchange, which emphasizes the importance of the residue for Al3+ interactions (Figure 5F).

results.result: SiNRAT transports diverse divalent metal ions (Mn2+, Ca2+, Mg2+) with micromolar affinity in a proton-uncoupled manner. Mn2+ transport saturates with Km ~14 µM, and Ca2+/Mg2+ compete with Mn2+ transport and are themselves transported, albeit weakly. No proton coupling was detected across multiple metal ions tested.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C27, C38-C41, and C48 collectively demonstrate broad divalent metal ion transport by SiNRAT without proton coupling. The data include saturation kinetics (C38), competition assays (C39), direct transport measurements (C40), and negative results for proton coupling (C48). The experimental evidence is consistent and well-replicated across multiple independent reconstitutions.

results.result: SiNRAT binds trivalent ions Al3+ and Ga3+, which are presumable substrates. Ga3+ inhibits Mn2+ transport specifically (not observed in EcoDMT), and ITC experiments show Al3+ binding with two binding constants in the low micromolar range.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C43-C45, and C47 provide evidence for trivalent ion binding, but direct transport could not be assayed due to technical limitations (membrane disruption). The ITC data (C45, C47) are complicated by Al3+ hydroxyl complex equilibria at neutral pH, and the Ga3+ competition data (C43) show incomplete inhibition. While binding is demonstrated, definitive assignment as transported substrates requires additional validation.

results.result: The cryo-EM structure of SiNRAT at 3.66 Å resolution reveals an occluded conformation closer to inward- than outward-facing state. The structure shares the conserved SLC11 family architecture and resembles the inward-occluded state of DraNRAMP (RMSD 1.57 Å) more than the outward-facing state (RMSD 2.71 Å).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C51, C53-C54, and C61-C67 are well-supported by high-quality cryo-EM data at 3.66 Å resolution. The structural comparisons with DraNRAMP conformations are quantitative (RMSD values) and the occluded state assignment is based on multiple structural features including gate residues and cavity accessibility. The map quality allowed unambiguous model building (C53).

results.result: The SiNRAT binding site is remodeled to accommodate trivalent cations with increased charge density. The site contains an elongated aqueous pocket (~10 Å long, 4-5 Å wide) three times larger than DraNRAMP, with consensus binding residues (Asp66, Ser68, Asn69, Ala238, Thr241) and an additional acidic residue (Asp140) that increases negative charge density.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C29-C30, C76-C79, C81-C83 are supported by structural data showing quantitative differences in binding site volume and composition. The identification of Asp140 as a conserved NRAT-specific residue that increases negative charge density is well-documented through structural comparison and sequence analysis. The replacement of methionine with threonine (C79) is structurally characterized.

results.result: Mutations of conserved binding site residues (Asp66, Asn69, Thr241) severely impair Mn2+ transport and Al3+ binding. The T241V mutant abolishes Al3+ binding in ITC experiments, confirming the importance of this residue for trivalent cation interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by functional data from multiple independent reconstitutions showing loss of transport (C84, C85) and loss of Al3+ binding (C86). The T241V result (C86) provides strong evidence linking the structural observations to Al3+ binding at the consensus site (C87). The mutations target residues identified in the structure as critical for ion coordination.

results.result: The S68A mutant shows distinct phenotypes for di- versus trivalent cations: Mn2+ transport is unaffected with similar kinetics and competition by Ca2+/Mg2+, but Ga3+ competition and Al3+ binding are abolished, suggesting different coordination requirements for trivalent ions.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 demonstrate a clear differential effect of the S68A mutation on divalent versus trivalent cation interactions. The data are internally consistent: normal Mn2+ transport (C88) with normal divalent ion competition (implied in C88) but loss of trivalent ion interactions (C89, C90). This supports the inference (C91) of distinct coordination modes, though the structural basis requires further investigation.

results.result: NRATs contain hallmark sequence features distinguishing them from classical NRAMPs: DPGN→DPSN on α1, A/CxxM→AxxT on α6 (replacing methionine with threonine), and a unique Ser68 (substituting Gly in other family members).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 and C70 are supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 (C32) and citations to previous work (C33, C34). The identification of these sequence signatures is consistent across the seven NRAT homologues identified (C31). The functional implications of these substitutions are tested experimentally in the mutagenesis studies.

results.result: Nanobody Nb1 binds SiNRAT at an extended extracellular interface (burying 1682 Å²), inhibits Mn2+ transport in a concentration-dependent manner, and stabilizes a conformation where α11 and α12 are detached from the core domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 and C58-C60 are supported by functional data (transport inhibition) and structural data (binding interface characterization). The incomplete inhibition (C50) is reasonably explained by mixed liposome orientation. The structural observations about α11/α12 detachment (C60) are based on comparison with EcoDMT and attributed to Nb1 stabilization.

results.result: The cryo-EM sample did not contain added transported ions due to amphipol reconstitution challenges and pH incompatibility with nanobody binding. Residual density between Asp66 and Ser68 presumably originates from water, Na+, or trace divalent metal ions.
results.evaluation: Claims C52 and C68 accurately describe experimental limitations and the speculative nature of the residual density assignment. The authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty about the density origin (C68) while using it cautiously to infer the ion binding position. This transparency about limitations is appropriate.

results.result: The broad substrate specificity of SiNRAT is consistent with other SLC11 family members (EcoDMT, DraNRAMP, EleNRMT), where mutagenesis typically retains Mn2+ transport capability, suggesting lower structural requirements for Mn2+ compared to other cations.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 and C98 are supported by citations to previous work and are consistent with the experimental observations in this study. The inference about lower structural requirements for Mn2+ (C94) is reasonable based on the cited mutagenesis studies, though it remains somewhat speculative. The comparison provides useful context for interpreting SiNRAT's properties.

results.result: The presumable trivalent ion binding region in SiNRAT was assigned by structural equivalence to other family members (DraNRAMP, ScaDMT, EleNRMT). Like NRMTs, the SiNRAT binding site is embedded in a larger aqueous cavity allowing both direct and water-mediated metal ion interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 appropriately acknowledge that the binding site assignment is based on inference from structural homology rather than direct observation of bound trivalent ions. The comparison with NRMTs (C101) is supported by structural data and citations. This approach is reasonable given the technical limitations preventing direct structure determination with bound Al3+.

results.result: Converting classical NRAMPs to Al3+ transporters by mutating only the consensus binding motif on α1 and α6 is likely insufficient. Previous unsuccessful attempts to convert EcoDMT to transport Mg2+ emphasize the importance of residues outside the narrow signature region for substrate selectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by citations to previous work and are consistent with the structural findings showing that Asp140 (outside the consensus motif) is important for Al3+ binding. The inference (C102) is reasonable based on the structural data and previous failed conversion attempts (C103). This highlights the complexity of substrate selectivity determinants.

results.result: The broad substrate specificity of SiNRAT contrasts with a previous study on rice NRAT1 showing selective Al3+ transport without Mn2+. This discrepancy may reflect different assay methods, and it remains unclear how Al3+ transport proceeds in the presence of other divalent ions.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 acknowledge an important discrepancy with previous work but offer only speculation (C106) about the cause. The uncertainty about physiological function (C107) is appropriate given the in vitro nature of the experiments and the lack of proton coupling that might provide selectivity in vivo. This represents an unresolved question requiring further investigation.

results.result: Background on the SLC11/NRAMP family and its branches (NRMTs, NRATs) based on established knowledge and previous work, including the authors' prior characterization of EleNRMT and the proposed role of NRATs in combating Al3+ toxicity in plants.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C8-C26 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to previous work. These claims establish the scientific foundation for the current study and are not primary findings of this manuscript. The citations appear appropriate and the background knowledge claims are consistent with the field.

results.result: Seven NRAT homologues were identified through phylogenetic analysis, and SiNRAT from S. italica was selected for study based on expression level and biochemical behavior. The protein was purified in DDM detergent, and transport experiments were conducted at neutral pH for technical reasons.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C36-C37, and C42 describe methodological choices and preliminary screening results. These are well-documented with appropriate figures and represent standard approaches for membrane protein characterization. The justification for neutral pH experiments (C42) is reasonable given the technical constraints.

results.result: SiNRAT contains 12 membrane-inserted helices like other eukaryotic SLC11 family members and EcoDMT, with Cα RMSD of 2.66 Å to EcoDMT. The unwound centers of the first helix of each repeat constitute the substrate binding site.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 and C55 describe conserved structural features of the SLC11 family confirmed by the SiNRAT structure. The RMSD value (C57) provides quantitative support for structural similarity. The binding site location (C55) is consistent with the LeuT-fold architecture common to this family.

results.result: Comparison of SiNRAT and DraNRAMPocc binding sites shows both have sealed water-filled paths to the metal ion binding site. In DraNRAMP, the Mn2+ ion is predominantly enclosed by protein residues (Asp56, Asn59, Ala53, Ala227, Met230) with octahedral coordination completed by water-mediated interaction with Gln378. In SiNRAT, Gln378 is replaced by Ser403.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 and C80 provide detailed structural comparison between SiNRAT and DraNRAMP binding sites. These comparisons are supported by structural data and citations to previous work on DraNRAMP (C72). The observations establish the baseline for understanding how SiNRAT differs from classical NRAMPs in accommodating different substrates.

results.result: Classical NRAMPs use a conserved methionine (soft ligand) to prevent alkaline earth metal ion binding, and mutating it to alanine converts Ca2+ into a substrate. NRMTs transport Mg2+ by increasing binding site volume to accommodate the hydrated cation without compromising Mn2+ transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 summarize previous work on substrate selectivity mechanisms in the SLC11 family, supported by appropriate citations. These provide important context for understanding the SiNRAT adaptations for trivalent cation transport. The claims accurately represent the cited literature.

results.result: The evolutionary distance of SiNRAT to classical NRAMPs is much smaller than to NRMTs.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic analyses. This evolutionary context is important for understanding why SiNRAT retains more structural similarity to classical NRAMPs than to the more distantly related NRMTs, despite having evolved different substrate specificity.

results.result: The findings are consistent with the proposed NRAT-mediated Al3+ detoxification mechanism in plants. The study provides the first structural insight into trivalent cation transport and reveals the architecture of a protein involved in plant defense against Al3+ toxicity. Future work could investigate whether NRAT overexpression increases plant Al3+ tolerance.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C112 provide appropriate context and perspective on the significance of the work. C108 correctly notes consistency with previous proposals (with appropriate citation), C109-C110 accurately summarize the study's contributions, and C111-C112 appropriately suggest future directions based on previous work showing that overexpression of Al3+ tolerance proteins can improve tolerance.
